lessons.title: The People: Founders and Cognitive Engineering

items: Attribute the field's core ideas to the people who introduced them
Know which name to cite for which claim
Card, Moran & Newell — Model Human Processor, GOMS and KLM, information foraging (with Pirolli). They made HCI predictive.
Ben Shneiderman — direct manipulation, the Eight Golden Rules, the visualisation mantra, Human-Centered AI. The field's most durable through-line from 1983 to 2026.
Donald Norman — the action cycle, the gulfs, affordances and signifiers, the error taxonomy. DOET is the discipline's shared vocabulary.
Jakob Nielsen — discount usability, heuristic evaluation, the five-user argument.
Bill Buxton — input devices, two-handed interaction, sketching in the design process.
Jef Raskin — Macintosh project origins; The Humane Interface (2000): modes are evil, habituation is destiny.
Alan Cooper — personas and goal-directed design.
Brenda Laurel — Computers as Theatre (1991): interaction as dramatic action, foundational for conversational and agent framing.
Terry Winograd — SHRDLU, then the turn: Understanding Computers and Cognition (with Flores, 1986), language as action.
Lucy Suchman — situated action; the standing critique of plan-based AI interaction.
Clayton Lewis — think-aloud method, cognitive walkthrough, cognitive accessibility.
Preece, Rogers & Sharp, and Alan Dix — authors of the two standard textbooks.
Lisanne Bainbridge — the ironies of automation
Nadine Sarter & David Woods — mode confusion and automation surprise
James Reason — error taxonomy and the Swiss-cheese model
Mica Endsley — situational awareness
Ed Hutchins — distributed cognition
Christopher Wickens — attention and workload models
Jonathan Grudin — the eight challenges, work/benefit disparity
Mark Ackerman — the socio-technical gap
Saul Greenberg & Carl Gutwin — workspace awareness
Judith and Gary Olson — distance matters
Robert Kraut — evidence-based community design
danah boyd, Amy Bruckman, Cliff Lampe — online social life and governance

cards.back: Model Human Processor, GOMS and KLM — they made HCI predictive rather than purely descriptive.
Direct manipulation, the Eight Golden Rules, the visualisation mantra, and Human-Centered AI.
The action cycle, the two gulfs, affordances and signifiers, and the slip/mistake error taxonomy.
Discount usability, heuristic evaluation, and the five-user argument.
The Humane Interface (2000) — modes are evil, habituation is destiny.
Situated action — plans are resources, not programs — and the founding critique of plan-based AI interaction.
The ironies of automation (1983): automating routine work destroys the skills needed for the exceptions.
Mode confusion and automation surprise in aviation — "How in the world did we ever get into that mode?"
Distributed cognition — Cognition in the Wild (1995). Cognitive processes span people, artefacts and representations.
The eight challenges of groupware, including the work/benefit disparity that explains most collaboration-tool failure.
The socio-technical gap — the divide between what must be supported socially and what can be supported technically.
Computers as Theatre (1991) — interaction as dramatic action, a foundation for conversational and agent framing.
Situational awareness — perception of elements, comprehension of meaning, projection of future state.

quiz.question: Whose work would you cite for "plans are resources for action, not programs"?
quiz.why: Suchman's Plans and Situated Actions (1987), the founding critique of plan-based intelligent interfaces.

quiz.question: Who made HCI a predictive engineering discipline rather than a descriptive one?
quiz.why: The Model Human Processor and GOMS let you compute expected task time before building anything.

quiz.question: Which pair explains why automating routine work makes exceptional cases harder to handle?
options: Bainbridge, with Sarter & Woods on mode confusion
quiz.why: Bainbridge's ironies of automation, with Sarter & Woods documenting the mode-confusion failures that follow.

items: Attribute the current human-AI research agenda to its authors
Eric Horvitz — mixed-initiative interaction, attention and interruption cost models
Saleema Amershi — the 18 Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, interactive machine learning
Krzysztof Gajos — cognitive forcing functions, adaptive interfaces
Zana Buçinca — overreliance and cognitive forcing
Gagan Bansal & Dan Weld — human-AI teams and complementary performance
Q. Vera Liao — the XAI question bank, transparency in the LLM age
Jenn Wortman Vaughan — interpretability and transparency
Cynthia Rudin — the interpretable-models-first position, in open debate with post-hoc XAI
Elena Glassman — variation theory, AI-resilient interfaces
Michael Terry & Carrie Cai — AI chains, prompt tooling, clinician onboarding
Meredith Ringel Morris — accessibility and AI, AGI interaction research
Qian Yang — AI as a design material
Hariharan Subramonyam — leaky abstractions in prompt-based design
Ben Green — algorithm-in-the-loop governance
Ken Holstein — human-AI complementarity in the wild
Mor Naaman — AI-mediated communication
Mina Lee — writing with LLMs, CoAuthor, the design space of writing assistants
J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira & Björn Hartmann — prompting usability
Park et al. — generative agents
Pattie Maes — the agents lineage and cognitive augmentation

cards.back: Mixed-initiative interaction and attention-cost modelling — the decision-theoretic answer to "should the agent act or ask?"
The 18 Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (CHI 2019) and interactive machine learning.
Cognitive forcing functions — interventions that reduce overreliance and that users dislike.
Human-AI team performance and complementarity — team beating the best member is rare and needs a model of when the AI errs.
The XAI question bank — reframing explanation as a user-needs design problem — and LLM-era transparency.
The interpretable-models-first position: use models that are inherently understandable rather than explaining opaque ones after the fact.
AI as a design material, and why human-AI interaction is uniquely difficult to design (CHI 2020).
Leaky abstractions — prompt-based development leaks model internals into UX decisions.
"Why Johnny Can't Prompt" (CHI 2023), the founding usability study of prompting.
CoAuthor and the design space of intelligent writing assistants.

quiz.question: Whose framework would you use to decide whether an agent should interrupt the user?
quiz.why: Horvitz gives the expected-utility rule weighing the value of acting against the cost of interrupting under uncertain intent.

quiz.question: Who argues against post-hoc explanation in favour of models that are interpretable by construction?
quiz.why: Rudin's position — and the book flags it as an open debate with the post-hoc XAI camp rather than a settled question.

cards.back: Chapters 6, 7, 12, 29, 33, 38, 39, 14, 36, then the capstone.

quiz.question: Which two industry resources does the book recommend as free, applied and evidence-linked?
options: Google PAIR Guidebook and Microsoft HAX Toolkit
quiz.why: PAIR and HAX are the two singled out as evidence-linked operationalisations of the human-AI research literature.

quiz.question: Which chapter does the recommended designer's fast path start with?
options: Chapter 6 — the action cycle and the gulfs
quiz.why: The gulfs are the master diagnostic tool; everything after is a gulf-bridging device, so the path starts there.
